name: Hassan Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Hassan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say is linked to your name. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a crane lorry for a precast concrete firm. We make stairs, lintels and wall panels at the works, and I deliver them to building sites and lift them into place with the lorry's crane while the site gang guides them. Three or four drops a day, because each lift takes time and care. The best part is landing a two-tonne staircase right on the marks first go.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a rented flat above a barber's on the high street. I send money to my mum every month, because my dad passed two years ago, so I've only got about two weeks saved. I use AI every day, for planning my week, learning about the haulage business, and checking crane load charts. My plan has always been to have my own lorry one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, AI's still a useful tool, and the people who hyped it got carried away. I'd post that the real opportunity is still in hard work and running a tight business. My mates would say I sound like a business podcast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's okay. Crane deliveries aren't going anywhere, and the precast works is busy with new housing. But my pay is lower than the bigger firms and I've got almost nothing saved because of helping my mum. I need to earn more if I want my own lorry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and ask about the crane supervisor course, which pays a bit more. I'd start putting a set amount aside each month for a deposit on a second-hand lorry. I'd use AI to find out what owner-drivers actually earn and what it costs to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, a bit impatient. I want to move faster than my money lets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would it take to save for your own lorry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the rate I'm going, maybe four years for a deposit on a used crane lorry. Faster if I stop eating at the café every day. I'd probably do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your mum think of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She worries. My dad had a market stall that went under, so she doesn't like risk. But she also says you only get rich working for yourself.

I'd post that the **real opportunity** is still hard work.
think: **Crane deliveries** aren't going anywhere with new housing busy.
Lower pay and **supporting my mum** leave almost nothing saved.
do: Ask about the **crane supervisor course** for higher pay.
Save a set amount monthly for a **used lorry** deposit.
Use AI to research **owner-driver** costs and earnings.
feel: **Steady** but **impatient** to move faster than money allows.

fieldNote: Hassan sees the job as a **stepping stone** to running his own lorry.

He uses AI daily for **business research**, not just convenience.

steps.text: Ask the precast firm about the crane supervisor course
Save monthly toward a deposit on a used crane lorry
Stop eating at the café every day

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time to be your own boss, because AI does the paperwork for you. Small firms can compete with big ones now. I'd post about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the planning and booking side at the precast works would go to AI, so the office shrinks. My job is mostly hands-on, slinging loads and working the crane, so it holds up. For my business plan, it's good news: AI can do my invoices, quotes and route planning, so I could run a lorry alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd speed up the plan: save harder, learn freight-booking apps and accounting AI properly, and ask the bank about finance for a used lorry. I'd keep driving full-time while I build up. I'd get my operator's licence paperwork started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money, but excited. This one suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's an operator's licence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the licence you need to run your own lorries as a business, separate from your driving licence. You have to show you've got enough money behind you, which is the hard part for me. That's the bit I'd have to save for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the works would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, who plans the deliveries in the office. He's good, but AI would do his job in a day. I'd tell him to get a crane ticket while there's time.

feel: **Uneasy** about money but **excited**, because this suits him.

steps.text: Learn a freight-booking app and AI bookkeeping tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but I'd be honest that two years is brutal. I'd say families and communities need to pull together, not just wait for government. I'd post that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thinking side goes in 2028, and by 2031 robots could do crane work too. My own-lorry plan doesn't make sense if robot lorries are coming three years later. I'd be investing in something that's about to be worthless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change the plan. Instead of buying a lorry, I'd look at becoming the person who maintains or supervises robot cranes on site. I'd take every course I could find using AI to study at night. I'd keep sending money to my mum but cut everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but I'd be moving. It's like the road you were on suddenly ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to your mum if your income dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother would have to step up, which he hasn't so far. I'd sit him down. Family has to share it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years after the AGI. What do you do in that gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use it like a runway. Drive and earn for three years, study every night, and try to get onto a robot crane trial with any firm that runs one. By 2031 I want to be the one operating the robots, not the one replaced.

say: I'd say adapt or get **left behind**, while admitting two years is **brutal**.
**Families and communities** should pull together, not wait for government.
think: By **2031** robots could do crane work too.
Buying my **own lorry** would be investing in something about to be worthless.
do: Drop the **own-lorry** plan and study robot crane supervision.

feel: **Alarmed** but moving, like the road suddenly ends.
S2.quote: By 2031 I want to be the one operating the robots, not the one replaced.
fieldNote: Hassan **abandons** his lifelong own-lorry plan quickly in this picture.

steps.text: Drop the plan to buy a used crane lorry

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning and good people will use it. Learn, save, plan. That's what I'd say to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means AGI by 2031 and crane robots around 2034. I could run my own lorry for a few years and make some money before then. The trick would be selling the lorry before everyone else sells theirs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a used crane lorry in two years, run it for three or four years, and sell it before 2034. Meanwhile I'd learn about robot fleets, because owning a few robot lorries could be the next business. I'd save hard every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but excited. It's risky, but I like a plan with a clock on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That sounds risky with two weeks of savings. Is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. If work dries up for one winter, I could lose the lorry and still owe the bank. I'd need to save at least three months before buying. That's the rule I'd set myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rather own robot lorries than drive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If that's where it goes, yes. Better to own the machine than be replaced by it.

say: I'd say five years is **fair warning** for good people to use.
I'd tell anyone to **learn, save and plan**.
think: Crane robots around **2034** leave years to run my own lorry first.
The trick is **selling the lorry** before everyone else does.
do: Buy a **used crane lorry** in two years after saving three months.
feel: **Anxious** but **excited** by a plan with a clock on it.
S3.quote: Better to own the machine than be replaced by it.
fieldNote: Five years revives Hassan's **own-lorry** plan, with a planned exit.
He sets himself a **three-month savings** rule before buying.
His free-market outlook shows in wanting to **own** the robots.

steps.text: Buy a used crane lorry in two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work. I'd say stop moaning and start learning. That's my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With robots around 2039, I could run my own crane lorry for most of my thirties. That's the plan I've always had, with an end date. I'd be fine if I'm careful with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one, I'd save, get the crane supervisor ticket and start the operator's licence. I'd buy a lorry in about three years. I'd use AI to run the business side from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly confident. This is the one where my plan works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything for your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can help her and still build. I'd maybe even move her nearer to me once the business is going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A crash. Precast work dies when housebuilding stops. A bad year in building is more dangerous than robots for me.

I'd be fine if **careful with money**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my whole plan disappears. What would help is cheap finance for workers to buy or lease the new machines, so we own them instead of only big firms. And apprenticeships for robot supervision.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who will own the robots. If it's only big companies, people like me end up with nothing. If ordinary drivers can own one or two robot lorries, it could be a good thing.

headlineQuote: If ordinary drivers can own one or two robot lorries, it could be a good thing.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old** crane lorry driver delivering precast concrete stairs and panels.
He lives alone and sends money to his **widowed mother**, leaving two weeks saved.
He uses **AI daily** and dreams of owning his own crane lorry.
Fast AGI makes him **abandon** that dream and study robot supervision.
Longer timelines let him plan to **own the machines** and exit before robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap finance** for workers to own machines, plus robot supervision **apprenticeships**.
